en: The Hymn of One Hundred and Eight Names of the Noble Lady Āryatārā. Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Noble Tārā.
On the beautiful and glorious Mount Potalaka, resplendent with various minerals,
It was filled with various trees and creepers, resounded with the warbling of various birds,
echoed with the gurgling of various waterfalls, teemed with various wild animals,
and was perfumed on all sides by various species of flowers.
It was endowed with various fruits as its heart-essence and resounded with the humming of six-legged bees;
it was filled with intoxicated elephants and made resonant by the sweet songs of *kiṃnaras*,
as well as by throngs of *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, and *gandharvas*.
It is constantly frequented by sages free from passion,
as well as by hosts of other bodhisattvas who are lords of the ten stages,
and by thousands of goddesses and vidyārājñīs, such as Āyatārā and others.
Surrounded by hosts of other wrathful kings, such as Hayagrīva and others,
the Blessed One Avalokita, who is dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings,
then dwelt there, glorious, seated upon a lotus-womb throne.
Endowed with great austerity and possessed of loving-kindness and compassion, he taught the Dharma in that vast assembly of gods. Then,
having approached him as he sat there, the mighty Vajrapāṇi arrived.
Endowed with supreme compassion, Avalokita asked: "O Sage,
these beings are sinking and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, distressed by the perils of thieves, serpents, lions, fire, elephants, tigers, and water."
"Bound by the snares of saṃsāra, which are characterized by passion, hatred, and darkness— tell me, O Great Sage, that by which they are liberated from saṃsāra.
When this was said, the glorious Avalokita, the Lord of the World, [responded].
He spoke these sweet words to the awakened Vajrapāṇi:
“Listen, O King of the Guhyakas, to the Mother of the World, the command of the Protector Amitābha, which has arisen through the power of his vow.”
Endowed with great compassion, they have uplifted the world for its deliverance;
resembling the rising sun and possessing the radiance of the full moon’s face,
these stars illuminate the trees, along with the gods, asuras, and humans.
"Shaking the three worlds and terrifying the yakṣas and rākṣasas, the goddess with the blue lotus in her hand said, 'Do not fear! Do not fear!
Speaking thus, I was brought forth by the Victors for the sake of protecting the world."
In the wilderness, amidst the clash of weapons, and in the midst of various terrors,
by the mere recollection of my names, I always protect sentient beings; O Protector,
I shall deliver them from the great ocean of manifold fears.
"Therefore, the bulls among sages, with palms joined in reverence and filled with respect and awe, sing of me in the world as 'the Savior.
Standing in the midst of the blazing sky, he spoke these words:"
Recite the *Nāmāṣṭaśataka*, which was proclaimed of old by the Jinas,
by the lords of the ten stages, the protectors, the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power—
[a recitation] that removes all evil, is meritorious, auspicious, and increases fame.
"O Great Sage, proclaim that which prevents the loss of wealth, increases health and nourishment, and is based upon loving-kindness toward all beings.
When this was said, the Blessed One, Avalokita, smiled.
Having surveyed all directions with a gaze radiating loving-kindness,
he raised his right hand, adorned with the marks of merit,
and said to him: "Excellent, excellent, O great ascetic of vast wisdom!"
Listen to the names, O highly fortunate one, you who are uniquely compassionate toward all beings;
by reciting them correctly, men shall become lords of wealth,
liberated from all diseases, and endowed with the qualities of all sovereignty.
Consumed by untimely death, they pass away and go to Sukhāvatī.
O hosts of gods, listen to me as I proclaim those [teachings];
may you rejoice in the true Dharma, and you shall become perfectly at peace.
Oṃ, O Locanā, Sulocanā, Tārā, Tārotsavā, you who have compassion for all sentient beings,
you who deliver all sentient beings, you with a thousand arms, you with a thousand eyes! Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Avalokita, the one who looks down.
And for all sentient beings, I am *phuṭ*! Svāhā!
Oṃ, pure one, utterly pure one, purifier, thorough purifier, daughter of the Sugata, whose heart is loving-kindness, stainless one, dark-blue one, you who possess a dark-blue form!
O you of great wisdom, most excellent one adorned with the most excellent, O vanquisher!
O Mahāraudrī, you of universal form, O you of great fame!
O you of the great splendor of the fire at the end of an eon, O you of great fame who sustains the world-system!

Sarasvatī, the large-eyed one, who increases wisdom, fortune, and intelligence; Oṃ! Bestower of steadfastness, bestower of nourishment, Svāhā! She whose form is desire, the syllable Oṃ, she who is intent on the welfare of all beings, the victorious one who delivers in battle. Tbh_30–31.
The goddess Prajñāpāramitā, noble Tārā, the enchanting one;
she who sounds like a drum, the full Vidyārājñī, the sweet-spoken one;
she with the moon-like face, Mahāgaurī, the unconquered one, clad in yellow garments.
Mahāmāyā, Mahāśvetā, she of great strength and prowess;
Mahāraudrī, Mahācaṇḍī, the slayer of wicked beings;
Praśāntā, Śāntarūpā, Vijayā, and Jvalanaprabhā.
Vidyunmālī, Dhvajī, Khaḍgī, Cakrī, and the one endowed with the bow as her weapon;
Jambhanī, Stambhanī, Kālī, Kālarātrī, Niśācarī;
Rakṣaṇī, Mohinī, Śāntā, Kāntā, Vibhāvinī, and Śubhā.
Brāhmaṇī, Vedamātā, Guhā, and Guhavāsinī;
Māṅgalyā, Śaṅkarī, Saumyā, Jātavedā, Manojavā;
Kāpālinī, Mahābhāgā, Sandhyā, Satyā, and Aparājitā.
The caravan leader with eyes of compassion, she who reveals the lost path;
the bestower of boons, the instructor, the teacher, in female form and of immeasurable prowess;
Śabalī, the Yoginī, the Siddhā, the Cāṇḍālī, the Immortal, the Eternal.
Blessed, meritorious, highly fortunate, and endowed with good fortune, she is lovely to behold;
she is terrifying to Death himself, formidable, fierce, and a performer of severe austerities;
she is devoted to the singular welfare of the world, a worthy refuge, and affectionate toward those who take refuge in her.
Vāgīśvarī, Śivā, Sūkṣmā, Nityā, the Mother of all objects (Sarvārthamātṛkā),
the accomplisher of all aims (Sarvārthasādhanī), Bhadrā, Goptrī, Dhātrī, Dhanañjayā,
Abhayā, Gautamī, Puṇyā, and Śrīmat— she who is the daughter of Lokeśvara.
Tārā possesses infinite qualities of name; she fulfills all hopes.
This hundred and eight names has been proclaimed for your benefit—a secret, marvelous, and hidden teaching, difficult even for the gods to obtain. (42–43)
It brings good fortune, creates auspiciousness, destroys all impurities,
pacifies all diseases, and bestows happiness upon all sentient beings.
The wise person who, being pure and composed, recites this three times after bathing—
In a very short time, one shall obtain the glory of sovereignty.
One who is suffering shall become happy; one who is perpetually poor shall become wealthy;
and one who is dull-witted shall become greatly wise and intelligent—of this there is no doubt.
One who is bound shall be released from bondage, and there shall be victory in legal disputes;
enemies shall turn into friends, as shall those with horns and those with fangs;
[this applies] in battle, in distress, in a fortress, or when beset by various fears.
Merely by remembering these names, one dispels all evils;
untimely death does not occur, and one attains vast prosperity.
For any great-souled person whatsoever, human birth becomes fruitful.
The man who, having risen early in the morning, recites this,
shall become long-lived and obtain prosperity for a long time.
Gods, nāgas, as well as yakṣas, gandharvas, and kaṭapūtanas—
Piśācas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and mothers of fierce splendor;
those who cause consumption and epilepsy, as well as kṣatakas, ākhorḍakas, and the like;
ḍākinīs, tārakas, pretas, skandas, māras, and the great grahas.
They do not even step upon his shadow, much less his physical body;
wicked beings do not afflict them, nor do diseases attack them.
Possessing great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), they even participate in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Endowed with all qualities of sovereignty, he prospers through sons and grandsons.
He shall be wise, mindful of his past lives, well-born, and pleasing in appearance;
full of joy, a great orator, and learned in all the scriptures.
"Attending upon spiritual friends and adorned with the thought of awakening,
he shall never be separated from the Buddhas wherever he may be reborn.
Thus ends the "One Hundred and Eight Names of the Noble Lady Ārya Tārā," spoken by the Buddha.
